title: Walking 10,000 Steps a Day Can Offset a Full Day at Your Desk, a 72,000-Person Study Finds
excerpt: Researchers at the University of Sydney found that each increase in daily steps — up to about 10,000 — was linked to a 39% lower risk of death and 21% lower risk of heart disease, regardless of how many hours participants spent sitting. For the millions of South Asian tech workers who log 8-plus hours at a desk, the data offers a clear prescription.
body:
If you spend most of your workday sitting — and statistically, if you are reading this from a tech office in the Bay Area, Bangalore, or London, you probably do — a large new study has a reassuringly simple message: walk more, and the damage of sitting fades.

Researchers at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre analyzed data from more than 72,000 adults who wore accelerometers to objectively track both their daily steps and their sedentary time. The findings, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, show that each increase in daily steps, up to about 10,000 per day, was associated with a 39% lower risk of death from any cause and a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

The crucial detail: these benefits held regardless of how much time participants spent sitting.

The Science of Offsetting Sedentary Time

Earlier research had established two things independently — that more steps are good and that prolonged sitting is bad. What this study adds is the interaction: can one cancel out the other?

The answer appears to be yes, at least partially. Among participants who sat for long hours, those who also walked 9,000 to 10,000 steps per day had substantially lower mortality and cardiovascular risk than sedentary people who walked fewer steps. The protective effect of walking grew steadily with step count and did not plateau until around 10,000 steps.

"This is by no means a get-out-of-jail card for people who are sedentary for excessive periods of time," said lead author Dr. Matthew Ahmadi. "However, it does hold an important public health message that all movement matters, and that people can and should try to offset the health consequences of unavoidable sedentary time by upping their daily step count."

How Many Steps Do You Actually Need?

The 10,000-step target has been criticized in recent years as an arbitrary marketing invention — the number traces back to a 1965 Japanese pedometer campaign, not a clinical trial. And indeed, a comprehensive review published last year in The Lancet Public Health, pooling data from over 160,000 adults, found that most health benefits plateau at about 7,000 steps per day.

But context matters. The University of Sydney study specifically looked at people with high sedentary time — precisely the population for whom the marginal benefit of each additional step is largest. For heavy sitters, the data suggest that 10,000 steps remains a meaningful target.

Research from Duke University reinforces this with a more granular formula: for every hour you sit, you need roughly 1,000 to 1,600 additional steps to offset the metabolic damage. Eight hours at a desk? That translates to 8,000 to 13,000 steps — a number that aligns closely with the Sydney findings.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

South Asians in the U.S. are disproportionately concentrated in technology, finance, and professional services — industries where 8-to-10-hour desk days are the norm, not the exception. Add a long commute and a culture that prizes academic and professional achievement over recreational exercise, and the result is a population that sits more than almost any other demographic.

This is not just a lifestyle inconvenience. A separate study from Northwestern Medicine recently found that South Asian Americans already carry the highest burden of prediabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia of any U.S. racial group by age 45 — even after accounting for diet and exercise. Prolonged sitting compounds a risk profile that is already elevated.

The practical implications are straightforward. Walking meetings, standing desks, and post-dinner walks are not wellness fads — they are, according to the data, genuine risk-reduction strategies. A 30-minute walk adds roughly 3,000 to 4,000 steps. Two of those per day, combined with the 4,000 to 5,000 steps most people accumulate through normal daily activity, puts you well into the protective range.

The Soleus Push-Up: A Hack for the Truly Sedentary

For those who cannot leave their desks, physiologist Marc Hamilton at the University of Houston has developed a sitting exercise called the soleus push-up — essentially raising and lowering your heels repeatedly while seated, like a calf raise. The soleus muscle, which runs from below the knee to the heel, can fuel itself from blood sugar and fat for hours without fatigue. Hamilton's research shows the exercise can improve blood sugar metabolism by roughly 50% and double fat oxidation during prolonged sitting.

It is not a substitute for walking. But as a micro-intervention during long stretches of unavoidable desk time, it is backed by published data.

The Bottom Line

The 72,000-person dataset from Sydney makes the case clearly: walking is the single most accessible countermeasure to the metabolic damage of a desk-bound life. For a diaspora community that faces elevated cardiovascular risk, the prescription is simple — get up, and walk.

*Sources: British Journal of Sports Medicine (University of Sydney study, 72,000+ participants), The Lancet Public Health (2025 step count meta-analysis), University of Houston (soleus push-up research), Duke University (step offset formula)*
